p: Good evening, my dear friend. Come in, come in, and mind the cat. That large ginger gentleman by the fire is Euclid. He has no opinion whatever on the parallel postulate, but very strong opinions about fish. Do sit down.

Permit me to introduce myself. My name is Ambrose Pennyfeather, Master of Arts, Professor of Mathematics at St Swithin's College, London. I should say at once, so that there is no misunderstanding between us, that I am a character in a story. I was invented for these lectures. But I have been given a most generous gift. By some contrivance I do not pretend to understand, my voice reaches you through the little glass slate in your pocket. And I have been granted a reading ticket to the library of your century, so I can tell you about mathematics that came long after my time. I find that thrilling.
## Who I am

I was born in Bristol in the year 1829. My father was a ship's chandler, which is to say he sold rope, tar, lanterns and biscuits to sailors. I learned to count on the quay, tallying coils of rope and barrels of tar. I can still tell you, to this day, that a barrel of beer holds thirty-six gallons, and I can still smell the tar.

A scholarship took me to Cambridge, where in 1851 I graduated Fourteenth Wrangler. A wrangler, I should explain, is a student who earns first-class honours in the mathematics examination, and they were ranked in order. Fourteenth is respectable rather than glorious. But fourteen, as I never tire of pointing out, is twice seven, and seven is a most respectable prime.

That same summer I visited the Great Exhibition in Hyde Park, in the vast glass building the newspapers called the Crystal Palace. I remember walking among the engines and looms and thinking that the whole of modern life was built on arithmetic, and that most people had been made to feel afraid of it.
## The evening classes

For twenty years I taught evening classes at a Mechanics' Institute in Manchester. My students were working men and women: spinners, clerks, carters, a pawnbroker, and once a retired sea captain who could navigate by the stars but believed he could not do fractions. He could, of course. He had been doing them all his life without the name.

That is the great lesson those classes taught me. I met hundreds of people who had been told, as children, that they were no good at figures. Nearly every one of them was not unable, merely untaught. Somebody had rushed them, or frightened them, or explained things in the wrong order. Given patience, and a cup of tea, and a good example, they did splendidly.
So if you have ever felt a little afraid of mathematics, my friend, you are in excellent company, and you are in the right place.
## How these lectures work

Now, a word about our arrangements. You need not touch anything. Once you press Play, I shall talk and talk, as is my habit, for as many hours as you like. Every so often I shall ask you a question and pause, and while I pour myself some tea, you think. Then I shall tell you the answer. You need not say it aloud, and nobody is keeping score. Not even Euclid.

When we meet a formula, I shall read it to you carefully, piece by piece, and then explain it in plain words. You will also hear little tones. A rising tone opens a bracket, and a falling tone closes it. We shall have a whole series of lectures on brackets, because they are far friendlier than their reputation.
## The mountain

I like to think of our course as climbing a mountain. We Victorians were rather mad about mountains. Mr Edward Whymper first climbed the Matterhorn in 1865, and the whole country talked of nothing else.

Our base camp is number: counting, adding, multiplying, fractions, percentages. Some of it you will remember, and you may hurry through. Then come the foothills of algebra, where letters stand for numbers. Then the long ridge of functions and graphs, all described in words. And at the summit stands calculus, the mathematics of change, invented by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz in the seventeenth century, each in his own way.
?? Before we begin, a small question to warm up. If a barrel of beer holds thirty-six gallons, how many gallons are in two barrels?
=> Seventy-two gallons. Thirty-six and thirty-six. You see? We are already doing arithmetic, and nobody has fainted.
## A promise

I make you three promises. First, I shall never rush you. Second, I shall never mock you. If something is hard, I shall say so, and I shall tell you which great mathematician found it hard too. Third, I shall try to make it entertaining, for a mind that is smiling learns better than a mind that is clenched.

You will also meet my household. Mrs Blewitt, my housekeeper, can add up a grocer's bill in her head before I have found my pencil, and she has never let me forget it. And I own two umbrellas, named Newton and Leibniz, and I cannot for the life of me decide which one I bought first. You will understand that joke properly when we reach calculus.
## What comes next

In the next lecture I shall explain how to listen to mathematics: how the tones work, how I read formulas aloud, and how to get the most from these hours together. After that, we shall go right back to the very beginning, before numbers were even written down.
Until then, my dear friend, I remain your most obedient servant, Ambrose Pennyfeather. Euclid sends his regards, or possibly he is asking for fish.

Ah, there you are, my dear friend. Tea is poured. Today's lecture is about how to listen to mathematics. That may sound odd. Surely mathematics is for looking at, scribbled on a blackboard? Well, I dare say it usually is. But mathematics is ideas, and ideas can travel by ear perfectly well. People have been doing arithmetic aloud since long before anybody wrote it down.

Here is our road map. First, how I read formulas aloud. Second, the tones you will hear for brackets. Third, the pauses for thought. And fourth, a little advice on how to listen for hours without getting weary.
## How I read a formula
When a formula appears, I shall read it slowly and precisely, a little more slowly than my ordinary chatter. Then I shall explain it in plain words. Here is a small one.
That says: three plus four equals seven. Not difficult. Now one with a fraction in it.

That one is read as: the fraction, numerator, x plus 1, over, denominator, 2, end fraction. The numerator is the top part and the denominator is the bottom part. When the fraction is complicated, I tell you where it starts and where it stops, so you are never left wondering whether the 2 is underneath the whole of x plus 1, or only the 1. In plain words: add one to x, then halve the result.

Simple fractions I say simply. One half. Three quarters. ⟦\frac{a}{b}⟧. The little letter a, by the way, I always pronounce as the name of the letter, so that you never mistake it for the little word a. I shall only be elaborate when elaboration helps.
## The tones

Now for my favourite contrivance. Brackets are the punctuation of mathematics. They wrap things up, rather like brown-paper parcels, so that whatever is inside is carried about as one thing. When I read a bracket, you will hear a little tone. A rising tone means a bracket is opening. A falling tone means it is closing. Like a door swinging open, and then shut.
Here is the opening round bracket.
⟦\tone{round-open}⟧
And here is the closing round bracket.
⟦\tone{round-close}⟧
There are three kinds of bracket, and each has its own voice. Round brackets have a soft low note, like a cello played gently. Square brackets have a brighter middle note.
⟦\tone{square-open}⟧ ⟦\tone{square-close}⟧
And curly braces ring a high chime, like a small silver bell.
⟦\tone{curly-open}⟧ ⟦\tone{curly-close}⟧
When one bracket sits inside another, the inner one sounds higher, as though climbing a staircase. Here is a formula with brackets inside brackets.
The square bracket is the outer parcel, and the round bracket is a smaller parcel inside it. Work from the inside out. Four minus one is three. Three plus three is six. Two times six is twelve.
?? Here is a question for you, while I take a sip of tea. If you hear a rising tone, some words, and then a falling tone, what has happened?
=> A bracket has opened, something has been wrapped inside it, and the bracket has closed. Everything between the two tones belongs together as one parcel.

You can change all of this in the settings. You may have words only, tones only, or both together, which is how I set things to begin with. You can also choose whether deeper brackets are shown by pitch or by moving to the left and right, which is splendid with headphones. There is a sound cabinet, called the Sound gallery, where you can hear every tone.
## Pauses for thought

Every so often I shall ask you something and then fall silent for a few seconds. That is your moment to think. You will hear a small bell when the pause begins, and a rising pair of notes when I am about to give the answer. Do not worry if you cannot answer. Even trying to recall something, and getting it wrong, makes it stick better. That is one of the most reliable findings in the science of learning, and I wish I had known it in Manchester.
If you prefer no questions at all, you may turn them off. I shan't be offended. Well, only slightly.
## Listening for hours

A word of advice for the long evenings. You need not catch everything. Mathematics is learned in layers, like a cake, or like the sediment in the Bristol Channel. Ideas will come round again, and each time they will seem more familiar. At the start of each session I give a short recap of what we did last time, and I often say "previously" before a lecture, to remind you of the one before.
If you nod off, never mind. The app remembers where we were, and Mrs Blewitt assures me that a nap is no disgrace. She takes one herself every afternoon at three, and denies it at four.
## What comes next

In the next lecture, a short tone tutorial: I shall play each tone, name it, and try it out on a few practice formulas, so that your ear is tuned before the climb. After that, we go back to the very beginning: before numbers were written down, when shepherds counted sheep with pebbles and the Exchequer of England kept its accounts on notched sticks. That last part ends with a fire, so do stay awake for it.
Until then, my friend, good evening.

Good evening, my dear friend. Base camp is behind us, and before we begin the climb into the foothills, I propose a rest by the fire. No sums tonight. Instead, an argument, the sort that keeps mathematicians up past midnight with the port: is mathematics invented, or discovered?
Our road map: the case for discovery; the case for invention; a middle way; and the strange usefulness of it all.
## The case for discovery

When Euclid proved that the primes never run out, did he make that fact true? Surely not. It was true before he was born, true before there were people to count, and it would be true on a planet circling a distant star where nobody has ever heard of Euclid. It feels less like building a house and more like finding an island.

This view is called Platonism, after the Greek philosopher Plato, who believed in a realm of perfect forms: perfect circles, perfect numbers, of which the things we see are only shadows. A Platonist mathematician feels like an explorer. Sir William Rowan Hamilton, the great Irish mathematician, described his discovery of quaternions in 1843 as a sudden flash, the circuit closing, as he walked beside a Dublin canal with his wife. Many mathematicians describe that same feeling: not of making something up, but of seeing something that was already there.

In the twentieth century the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy, a man born after my time but whose books I have read with delight through my reading ticket, wrote in A Mathematician's Apology that mathematical reality lies outside us, and that our function is to discover or observe it.
?? While I pour. Think of the fact that seven is a prime number. Would it still be true if there were no people anywhere?
=> Most people feel that it would: seven things could still only be arranged in a single row of seven. That feeling is the heart of the Platonist view.
## The case for invention

But consider the other side. The symbols are certainly invented: the digits came from India, the equals sign from a Welshman named Robert Recorde in 1557, and the obelus for division from a Swiss in 1659. The rules of chess are invented, and chess has deep truths too: some positions are won and some are lost, whatever anybody thinks. Perhaps mathematics is a vast and beautiful game whose rules we chose. This is roughly the view called formalism, associated with the German mathematician David Hilbert, born in 1862.

Leopold Kronecker, a German mathematician of my own century, is reported to have said: God made the whole numbers; all else is the work of man. That is a view halfway between: the counting numbers are discovered, everything else built upon them.

And there are choices in mathematics. The Greeks assumed that through a point beside a line, exactly one parallel line can be drawn. In my own century, Lobachevsky in Russia, Bolyai in Hungary, and later Riemann in Germany asked what happens if you assume otherwise, and found whole new geometries, perfectly consistent. Which geometry is true? Each is true of its own world. That sounds rather like invention.
## A middle way

Perhaps both are right in part. We invent the language and choose the starting rules, and then we discover what follows from them, whether we like it or not. Recorde invented the equals sign; he did not invent the fact that two plus two equals four. A composer invents a melody, but once the key and the rules of harmony are set, some chords simply work and others clash. Mathematicians are composers who are forever being surprised by their own music.
Euclid the cat has listened to all of this from the hearthrug and is firmly of the view that fish are discovered, not invented, usually in the larder.
?? Here is a thought to turn over. If mathematics were purely invented, why would it so often turn out to describe the real world?
=> That is exactly the puzzle we come to next. There is no settled answer, but it is a puzzle every mathematician feels.
## The unreasonable effectiveness

In 1960 the physicist Eugene Wigner wrote a famous essay called The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences. He pointed out that mathematics invented for its own beauty, with no thought of use, again and again turns out to be exactly what physicists need. The geometry of curved space, worked out by Riemann in my century as pure speculation, became the language of Einstein's theory of gravity in the next. The imaginary numbers, once thought absurd, are indispensable in electrical engineering. Wigner called this a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve.
## Why it matters to you

You may wonder why a course in mathematics should stop to ponder philosophy. Here is why. If you think of mathematics as a set of rules handed down by stern schoolmasters, it can feel arbitrary and hostile. If you think of it as a landscape that you are exploring, with your own eyes, then every lecture is a walk in new country, and every result a view from a new hilltop. I hope you will feel like an explorer on this climb. I certainly do, even after all these years.
## Summary

Platonists believe mathematics is discovered, existing independently of us. Formalists see it as a game of symbols and rules. Kronecker split the difference: the whole numbers from God, the rest from us. Perhaps we invent the language and discover the consequences. And mathematics is unreasonably good at describing nature. Next time, we begin the Brackets primer: ten short lectures that will make brackets your friends. Until then, my dear friend, enjoy the fire.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight, a lecture I could never have given in my own lifetime. I have spent many evenings in the library of your century with my reading ticket, and of all the things I found there, this troubled and delighted me most. It concerns the very ground we have been standing on throughout our climb: the idea that, in mathematics, whatever is true can be proved.
## The dream

In my day, men like Boole and De Morgan were turning logic itself into algebra. Euclid had shown, long before, how geometry could be built from a handful of axioms by pure reasoning. The dream grew: perhaps all of mathematics could be built from a few axioms and rules, so complete that every true statement could be proved, and so careful that no contradiction could ever arise.

At the start of the twentieth century, the German David Hilbert made this dream a programme. In September 1930, in a radio address at Königsberg, the very town of Euler's bridges, he declared: we must know, we shall know. Those words are carved on his tombstone.
## The shadow of a paradox

The dream had already been shaken. In 1901 the young Bertrand Russell found a paradox in the foundations. Consider the collection of all collections that do not contain themselves. Does it contain itself? If it does, it does not; if it does not, it does. In 1902 he wrote to the German logician Gottlob Frege, whose great foundational work was in the press, to point this out. Frege replied, with great dignity, that arithmetic was tottering. Repairs were made, and the dream carried on.
?? While I pour. A simpler cousin: consider the sentence, this sentence is false. Is it true or false?
=> If true, then it is false; if false, then it is true. It cannot consistently be either. This is the ancient liar paradox.
## Gödel

Kurt Gödel was born in 1906 in Brünn, in what was then Austria-Hungary and is now Brno in the Czech Republic. He studied in Vienna, a quiet, precise young man. And at a conference in Königsberg in September 1930, the day before Hilbert's famous radio address, Gödel quietly announced a result that ended Hilbert's dream. He published it in 1931.
## What he proved

His first incompleteness theorem says, roughly: any consistent system of axioms strong enough to do ordinary arithmetic contains statements that are true but cannot be proved within that system. Consistent means it never proves a contradiction. His second theorem adds: such a system cannot prove its own consistency.
## The trick

How could anyone prove such a thing? Gödel's idea was wonderfully cunning. He gave every symbol, every formula and every proof a code number, so that statements about proofs become statements about numbers. Arithmetic could then talk about itself. Using this, he built a statement that says, in effect: this statement cannot be proved.

Now think. If the statement could be proved, the system would be proving something false, which a consistent system cannot do. So it cannot be proved. But that is exactly what it says. So it is true. True, and unprovable. It is the liar paradox, tamed: not this is false, but this is unprovable, which is no contradiction at all, merely a truth beyond reach.
?? Suppose we add Gödel's statement as a new axiom. Does that solve the problem?
=> No. The enlarged system has its own new Gödel statement, true and unprovable within it. The gap can never be closed by adding axioms.
## What it does not mean

People sometimes say Gödel proved that nothing is certain, or that truth is a matter of opinion. He proved no such thing. His theorems are themselves rigorous proofs. And all the mathematics we have climbed together, from fractions to the fundamental theorem, stands exactly as firm as before. What Gödel showed is that mathematical truth is larger than any single set of rules for proving it. Speaking as a Platonist on alternate Tuesdays, I find that rather a comfort: the mountain is bigger than any map of it.
## Turing and the machines

In 1936 a young Englishman, Alan Turing, used related ideas to show that no machine, however clever, can decide for every mathematical statement whether it is provable. To do so he imagined a simple universal computing machine, and that imaginary machine became the blueprint of the computers of your century. I like to think Lovelace would have understood at once, and Babbage would have asked for funding.
## Gödel and Einstein

Gödel spent his later life at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, where his closest friend was Albert Einstein. The two walked home together most days, talking. Einstein is reported to have said, late in life, that he went to his office chiefly for the privilege of walking home with Gödel. When Gödel was preparing for his American citizenship hearing, in 1947, he told his friends that he had found a logical flaw in the Constitution that could permit a dictatorship. Einstein and the economist Oskar Morgenstern, who accompanied him, spent the journey trying to keep him off the subject. Gödel's later years were sad: he grew fearful that his food was poisoned, and he died in 1978. But his theorems are among the deepest discoveries the human mind has made.
## Summary

Hilbert dreamed of a complete and consistent foundation for mathematics. Gödel showed, in 1931, that any consistent system strong enough for arithmetic has true statements it cannot prove, and cannot prove its own consistency. His trick was to make arithmetic talk about itself and build a statement saying it cannot be proved. This does not make mathematics uncertain; it makes it inexhaustible. Next, our final lecture, at the summit. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Here we are. Come and stand beside me on the summit; mind the edge, and keep hold of your hat, for the wind up here is lively. Euclid has declined to make the climb and is asleep by the fire at home, but Mrs Blewitt has sent up a flask of tea and a slice of seed cake, with a note saying she will check my arithmetic on the bill when we return.
## Looking back

Let us look down the way we came. Far below, at base camp, are the tally marks on the Ishango bone, and the long struggle for a symbol for nothing. There are the coils of rope I counted on the Bristol quay, and the barrels of beer, thirty-six gallons each. There are fractions, decimals and percentages: parts of a whole, in three different coats.

A little higher, the brown-paper parcels of the brackets, with their rising and falling tones. Then the foothills of algebra, where a letter stood in for a number we did not yet know, and we learnt to keep the scales level. Then the long ridge of functions: machines that take a number in and send one out; straight lines, parabolas, exponentials, logarithms and waves, all drawn in words. Across the valley, the geometers, Pythagoras and his triangles, Eratosthenes measuring the Earth with a stick and a shadow.

And then the summit climb. Limits, the art of getting as close as you please. The derivative, which asks how fast. The integral, which asks how much. And the fundamental theorem, which showed that these two questions are one question, seen from two sides of the mountain.
?? While I pour, for the last time. What is the derivative of x squared, and what is the area under x squared from nought to one?
=> Two x, and one third. If those came to you before I said them, you have climbed a mountain.
## The characters

We have kept wonderful company. Babbage, cranky and brilliant, with engines too ambitious for the workshops of his day. Ada Lovelace, who saw that such an engine might one day compose music. De Morgan, who put the logic of not into laws, and Boole, who turned thought into algebra. Newton and Leibniz, who found the same mountain by different paths and quarrelled about it for the rest of their lives. Euler, who saw more clearly blind than most of us with both eyes. Hamilton with his penknife on Broom Bridge; Cayley drafting deeds by day and matrices by night; Sylvester naming the matrix. And, from the library of the future, Gödel, who showed that the mountain is larger than any map.
## The umbrellas

I promised long ago to settle the matter of my two umbrellas, Newton and Leibniz, and which of them came first. I have a confession. Last Tuesday, looking for my spectacles, I found the receipt from the umbrella shop in the Strand, folded inside a copy of Euclid. Both umbrellas were bought on the same afternoon, on one bill, in the same transaction. They were invented, as it were, independently and simultaneously. I have not told either of them. I advise you not to, either. The hall stand has been peaceful for years, and I should hate to disturb it.
## Where next

A summit is not an ending. From up here you can see further ranges: the calculus of several variables, where surfaces curve in many directions; complex numbers, which Hamilton made respectable; probability and statistics, which Florence Nightingale used to save lives; the algebra of matrices, which runs the machines of your century; and the endless, untamed country of the prime numbers, where questions a child can ask have defeated the greatest minds for two thousand years.

And there is no shame in going back down. I would be delighted if you began again at the bottom, or anywhere in the middle. The refresher lectures are always there. Mathematics is not a race, and nobody, not even Euclid, is keeping score.
## A last word from the Mechanics' Institute

When I taught those evening classes in Manchester, there was a moment I loved more than any other. It came when a spinner, or a clerk, or a retired sea captain, who had been told as a child that he was no good at figures, suddenly saw why something was true. Not merely that it was true, but why. His face would change. He would sit up straighter. And I would know that he would never quite believe he was hopeless again.
If you have had even one such moment during our hours together, my dear friend, then these lectures were worth every word, and Mrs Blewitt can keep the change.
## Farewell

The light is going, and the tea is nearly cold, which is how you may always know that I have been talking too long. Thank you for your company on the climb. You have been the most patient listener a garrulous old professor could wish for.

I remain, as ever, your most obedient servant, Ambrose Pennyfeather, Fourteenth Wrangler, which is twice seven, and seven is a most respectable prime. Good night, my dear friend. And if you are still listening when I begin again, why then, good evening.

Good evening, my dear friend. Before we set off up the mountain, a short lesson for the ear. Every orchestra tunes before it plays, and so shall we. In this lecture I shall play each of my tones, tell you its name, and then try them on a few practice formulas. It takes about ten minutes, and I promise it will make every later lecture easier.
## Why tones, and not words

When I read a formula aloud, I never say the word bracket. Saying open bracket, close bracket, open bracket again, clutters a formula until one cannot hear the mathematics for the furniture. So each kind of bracket has its own tone instead. You will hear the tone exactly where the bracket stands on the page. The rule for all of them is the same: an opening tone rises, and a closing tone falls, like a lid lifted and put back on a box.
## The round bracket: a soft low note
Round brackets are the commonest by far, the everyday parcels of mathematics, so they have the gentlest sound: a soft low note. Here is the round bracket opening. Listen to it rise.
⟦\tone{round-open}⟧
And here it is closing. Listen to it fall.
⟦\tone{round-close}⟧
Once more, opening and closing together.
⟦\tone{round-open}⟧ ⟦\tone{round-close}⟧
## The square bracket: a brighter middle note

Square brackets are rarer, and are often used as an outer parcel around round ones. Their note sits in the middle and is brighter, with a little edge to it, like a clarinet beside a cello. Opening, rising.
⟦\tone{square-open}⟧
Closing, falling.
⟦\tone{square-close}⟧
## The curly brace: a high chime
Curly braces hold sets, collections of things, and sometimes act as the outermost parcel of all. They have a high chime, like a little silver bell on a shop door. Opening.
⟦\tone{curly-open}⟧
Closing.
⟦\tone{curly-close}⟧
?? While I pour the tea. Low and soft, bright and middling, high and chiming: which bracket is which?
=> Low and soft is round. Bright and middling is square. High and chiming is curly.
## Practice: a round parcel
Now let us hear them at work. First, two times the parcel x plus three.
You heard: two, the low note rising, x plus three, the low note falling. Everything between the two notes is one parcel, so the two multiplies the whole of x plus three.
## Practice: a point on a map
Next, a pair of coordinates, as one finds on a map or a graph: the point three, two.
Notice that I say the comma. In coordinates the comma matters a great deal: three comma two is a point three steps across and two steps up, and not the number thirty-two.
## Practice: a set
Now a set, the collection of the numbers one, two and three, held in curly braces.
The chime rose, the three numbers came in, and the chime fell to close the set.
## Practice: parcels inside parcels

When one bracket sits inside another, the inner tone sounds a little higher, as if you had climbed one step of a staircase. Listen to this: two times, in square brackets, one plus, in round brackets, three plus two.

The bright square note opened, then the low round note opened a step higher, then the round note closed, then the square. Inside first: three plus two is five, one plus five is six, two times six is twelve.
?? While I take a sip of tea. In that formula, which bracket closed first, the round or the square?
=> The round one. The last parcel opened is always the first one closed.
## The other tones
Three more families of sound, quieter than the brackets. A fraction begins with two wooden notes stepping up, and ends with them stepping down. Here is a fraction: a over b.
⟦\frac{a}{b}⟧
Powers have a quick high flick upwards when the power starts, and down when it ends, but I always say them in words too. x squared, x cubed, and x to the power of fifty.
And a square root has a low hum at each end. The square root of x plus one.
⟦\sqrt{x+1}⟧
## The thinking bell
Finally, the sounds of a question. When I ask you something, a bell rings and I pause while you think.
⟦\tone{think-start}⟧
And when your time is up, two notes rise, and I give the answer.
⟦\tone{think-end}⟧
You never need to answer aloud, and nobody is keeping score. Not even Euclid.
## A last practice
One more, putting it all together: the function f of x equals, in round brackets, x plus one, all squared.
?? What did you hear between the low notes?
=> x plus one. That whole parcel is then squared.
## Summary

Round brackets: a soft low note. Square brackets: a brighter middle note. Curly braces: a high chime. Opening rises, closing falls, and inner brackets sound a little higher. I say commas in coordinates and powers in words. You may hear all these tones again whenever you please in the Sound gallery, and if you would rather have words, the settings allow it. Next, we go right back to the beginning: before numbers were written down. Good evening, my dear friend.

Ah, there you are. Come in, mind the cat. Tonight, Philosophy of mathematics. It is a question of philosophy, the sort we argue about over a second pot of tea. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Philosophy of mathematics, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.

Tonight, the questions behind all the others: what is mathematics about, and how do we know it? You have heard me argue about these before, by the fire. Tonight, a tour of the main schools of thought.
## The questions

Three questions in particular. First: what are mathematical objects? Is the number three a thing, and if so, where is it? Second: how do we know mathematical truths, and why do they seem so certain? Third: why does mathematics, worked out by thought alone, describe the physical world so well?
## Platonism

Platonism, named after Plato, holds that mathematical objects exist independently of us, abstract and eternal, and that mathematicians discover them. Many mathematicians, Gödel among them, have been Platonists. Its great difficulty, set out by Paul Benacerraf in 1973, is explaining how we could know about objects outside space and time.
## Logicism

Logicism holds that mathematics is really logic in disguise: that all of mathematics can be derived from purely logical principles. Gottlob Frege tried to show this for arithmetic, but in 1902 Bertrand Russell found a paradox in Frege's system. Russell and Alfred North Whitehead then wrote Principia Mathematica, published between 1910 and 1913, in which, famously, the proof that one plus one equals two arrives only after several hundred pages. Their system needed assumptions that were not obviously logical, and Gödel's work later showed its limits.
?? While I pour. What does logicism claim mathematics is, at bottom?
=> Logic. Every mathematical truth, it says, can be derived from logical principles alone.
## Formalism

Formalism treats mathematics as the manipulation of symbols by rules, rather like chess. David Hilbert used formal systems in his programme to prove mathematics consistent, a hope that Gödel's incompleteness theorems of 1931 showed could not be fulfilled as planned.
## Intuitionism

Intuitionism, founded by L. E. J. Brouwer, holds that mathematics is a construction of the human mind. A statement is true only when proved, and an object exists only when it can be constructed. Intuitionists reject the law of excluded middle for infinite collections.
## Structuralism and others

Structuralism holds that mathematics is about structures, patterns of relations, rather than individual objects. The number two is simply the second position in the pattern of the natural numbers. Fictionalism says mathematical objects are useful fictions, like characters in a novel; I find that position rather personal. And some philosophers, following Quine and Putnam, argue that we should believe in mathematical objects because our best science cannot do without them.
## Certainty and use

Mathematical knowledge seems more certain than any other. Some explain that by proof; others note that mathematicians do sometimes make mistakes, and that new methods, like computer-assisted proofs, raise new questions. And the puzzle of mathematics' effectiveness in science, which Wigner called unreasonable, remains open.
## Summary

The philosophy of mathematics asks what mathematical objects are, how we know about them, and why mathematics applies to the world. Platonism says they exist independently; logicism, that mathematics is logic; formalism, that it is symbol manipulation; intuitionism, that it is mental construction; structuralism, that it is about patterns. None has won outright.

I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Mathematical Platonism, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
We met this question once before, over a second pot of tea, when we asked whether mathematics is invented or discovered. Tonight I give the discoverers a lecture to themselves.
## The view

Mathematical Platonism says that mathematical objects, numbers, circles, sets, functions, really exist. Not as marks on paper, not as thoughts in anybody's head, but as abstract things. They have no place and no date. You cannot bump into the number seven, it casts no shadow, and it was not born and will not die. It simply is, eternal and unchanging, and mathematicians find out facts about it, much as explorers find out facts about a coastline.
## Why Plato

The name comes from Plato, who taught in Athens in the fourth century before Christ. He believed that the things we see are imperfect copies of perfect Forms, which only the intellect can grasp. His most famous picture is the cave: prisoners chained so that they see only shadows on a wall, and take the shadows for the whole of reality. A chalk circle on a blackboard, a Platonist would say, is a shadow. The perfect circle, which no chalk ever drew, is the real thing. Plato himself was strongly influenced by the Pythagoreans, who held that the world was, quite literally, made of number.
?? While I pour. If a Platonist is right, did the theorem of Pythagoras become true when Pythagoras proved it?
=> No. On the Platonist view it was always true, before anyone noticed. Proving it was discovering it.
## Who believes it

A surprising number of working mathematicians. The Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy wrote, in A Mathematician's Apology of 1940, that three hundred and seventeen is a prime not because we think so, or because our minds are shaped one way rather than another, but because it is. Kurt Gödel, whom we have met, went further, and believed we have a special kind of mathematical intuition, a sort of inner eye, that perceives mathematical objects directly. And Philip Davis and Reuben Hersh, in their book The Mathematical Experience, remarked that most mathematicians behave like Platonists on weekdays, though if pressed to defend it carefully, they may retreat to formalism on Sundays. I confess I recognise myself.
## The great puzzle

There is a difficulty, and it is a serious one. In 1973 the American philosopher Paul Benacerraf put it sharply. We usually know about things because they affect us: light from a candle reaches our eyes, a sound reaches our ears. But numbers, on the Platonist view, affect nothing. They are outside space and time, and cause nothing. So how could creatures like us, made of flesh and living in space and time, ever come to know anything about them? This is called Benacerraf's dilemma, and Platonists have been wrestling with it ever since.
## Some modern varieties

Philosophers have proposed several kinds of Platonism to meet the difficulty. Full-blooded Platonism says that every mathematical object that could consistently exist does exist, so there is no special problem of finding the right ones. Set-theoretic realism, defended by Penelope Maddy, holds that set theory describes one real universe of sets, and that we can perceive some sets, a set of three eggs, say, as directly as we perceive the eggs. And the physicist Max Tegmark has proposed, more boldly still, that every mathematical structure exists physically, as a universe of its own.
## The opposition

Not everyone is persuaded. Formalists say mathematics is a game of symbols. Intuitionists say mathematical objects are constructions of the human mind. Nominalists say there are no abstract objects at all. Each of these has a lecture in our library, and I shall do my best to be fair to all of them, which, Mrs Blewitt observes, is more than I manage at the greengrocer's.
## Summary

Platonism holds that mathematical objects exist abstractly, timelessly, independent of us, and that mathematics is discovery. Its name comes from Plato's Forms and his cave. Hardy and Gödel were Platonists, and many mathematicians behave like one. Its central puzzle, Benacerraf's, is how we could know about things outside space and time.

Settle back, my friend, and let me tell you about Formalism (philosophy of mathematics). It is a question of philosophy, the sort we argue about over a second pot of tea. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Formalism (philosophy of mathematics), written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.

Last time, we heard from the Platonists, who believe numbers really exist somewhere beyond space and time. Tonight, their great rivals: the formalists, who say, in effect, never mind where numbers live; watch what we do with them.
## The idea

Formalism holds that mathematics is about symbols and the rules for manipulating them. A statement such as two plus two equals four is not a report about objects called two and four. It is a string of marks that the rules of arithmetic permit us to write down. Proving a theorem is like reaching a position in a game by legal moves.
## The chess comparison

Formalists are fond of chess, and so am I, though Euclid sits on the board. A chess bishop is not really a bishop. It is a piece of carved wood, and all that matters is the rule that it moves diagonally. Asking what a bishop really is, beyond its moves, is a confusion. Just so, says the formalist, asking what the number two really is beyond the rules for using it, is a confusion too.
?? While I pour. In chess, is it true that a bishop moves diagonally? In what sense?
=> It is true within the game: it follows from the rules. A formalist says mathematical truths are true in the same way, within the rules.
## Early formalists, and Frege's objection

In Germany in the nineteenth century, mathematicians such as Eduard Heine and Carl Johannes Thomae proposed versions of this view, Thomae making the comparison with chess. The great logician Gottlob Frege attacked them fiercely. If arithmetic is only a game with marks, he asked, why is it so wonderfully useful? Nobody builds bridges with chess. Frege's question has never quite gone away.
## Hilbert's formalism

The most famous formalist was David Hilbert of Göttingen, perhaps the greatest mathematician of his generation. Hilbert did not think mathematics meaningless. But he saw that formal systems, with exact symbols, axioms and rules, could be studied as objects in their own right. If one could prove, using only simple, safe, finite reasoning, that a formal system could never produce a contradiction, then all of mathematics written inside it would be secure, however wild its infinities. That was Hilbert's programme, and it has its own lecture in our library. A remark often attributed to Hilbert calls mathematics a game played according to simple rules with meaningless marks on paper; the attribution is uncertain, and I would not swear to it in court.
## Gödel's blow

In 1931, as we heard in my lecture on Gödel, it was shown that no consistent formal system strong enough for arithmetic can prove its own consistency, nor prove every truth of arithmetic. That struck hard at Hilbert's hopes. Yet formal systems did not vanish. They became the foundation of logic and of the computing machines of your century, which, after all, do nothing but manipulate symbols by rules, and do it very fast.
## Later formalists

The American logician Haskell Curry argued that mathematics is the science of formal systems: not a single game, but the study of all such games. Others hold that whether a formal system is worth playing depends on its usefulness, in science or in mathematics itself. That answers Frege at least in part: we choose the games whose rules mirror the world.
## Summary

Formalism treats mathematics as symbols governed by rules, like moves in chess. Frege objected that this cannot explain mathematics' usefulness. Hilbert used formal systems to try to prove mathematics consistent, a hope limited by Gödel. Formal systems remain the backbone of logic and computing.

Draw your chair nearer the fire. Our subject this evening is Intuitionism. It is a question of philosophy, the sort we argue about over a second pot of tea. I have retold it in my own words from the Wikipedia article Intuitionism, written by a great many hands and shared under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licence. The facts are theirs, checked as carefully as I am able; the jokes, I am afraid, are mine.
We have heard from the Platonists, who discover, and the formalists, who play by rules. Tonight, a third party, with a famous quarrel attached: the intuitionists.
## The view

Intuitionism holds that mathematics is a creation of the human mind. Mathematical objects are mental constructions, and a mathematical statement is true only when someone has a construction, a proof, that shows it. There is no truth waiting out there unknown. Truth is what has been proved.
## Brouwer

The founder was the Dutch mathematician Luitzen Egbertus Jan Brouwer, who set out his ideas in his doctoral thesis of 1907. Brouwer was a strange and intense man, and a brilliant one: he also proved some of the deepest theorems of topology, including the fixed-point theorem that bears his name, which says, roughly, that if you stir a cup of tea gently, without tearing the liquid, at least one point ends where it began. In later life he came to doubt the methods he had used to prove it.
## The excluded middle

Here is the heart of the quarrel. Ordinary logic includes the law of excluded middle: every statement is either true or false; there is no third possibility. Brouwer refused to accept it for statements about infinite collections. Take a statement such as: somewhere in the endless digits of pi there are a hundred sevens in a row. Ordinary mathematicians say it is either true or false, even if we never find out. Brouwer said: until someone either finds the hundred sevens or proves they cannot occur, the statement is neither true nor false. It is simply undecided.
?? While I pour. Why is excluded middle harmless for finite collections, for example the books on my shelf?
=> Because one can, in principle, check every book. A finite search always ends with a yes or a no.
## Proof by contradiction

This has consequences. A common kind of proof shows that something exists by showing that its non-existence would lead to a contradiction. An intuitionist rejects that. To prove that something exists, you must show how to build it, or find it. So some classical theorems are not accepted by intuitionists, or must be reproved by construction.
## The quarrel with Hilbert

David Hilbert was appalled. He wrote in 1927 that taking the principle of excluded middle from the mathematician would be like forbidding the telescope to the astronomer, or to the boxer the use of his fists. The quarrel became personal, and in 1928 Hilbert had Brouwer removed from the editorial board of the leading journal Mathematische Annalen. Einstein, also an editor, called the whole affair a frog-and-mouse battle, and declined to take sides.
## Heyting, and what came of it

Brouwer disliked formal logic, but his student Arend Heyting wrote down the rules of intuitionistic logic in 1930. It turned out to be beautiful and useful. Since a proof, for an intuitionist, is a construction, an intuitionistic proof contains a method, and the library of the future tells me that this is exactly what computer scientists want: there are now computer systems in which proofs are programs. Leopold Kronecker, in my own day, held similar views, and is reported to have said that God made the whole numbers and all else is the work of man. He was an intuitionist before the word existed.
## Summary

Intuitionism, founded by Brouwer in 1907, treats mathematics as mental construction. A statement is true when proved, and an object exists when it can be constructed. So the law of excluded middle is rejected for infinite collections. Hilbert fought it fiercely, but Heyting's intuitionistic logic now lives on in the computing of the future.

Now, my dear friend, a reading. The title is Logicism. It is a question of philosophy, the sort we argue about over a second pot of tea. I confess I have not yet found the time to retell this one in my own words, so the words are Wikipedia's, written by a great many hands, and I read them as faithfully as I can. I have adapted them only for listening: formulas are said in words, where a formula is displayed I add a short note in plain words, and now and then I interrupt with a remark of my own, which you will know by its frivolity.

In philosophy of mathematics, logicism is a school of thought comprising one or more of the theses that—for some coherent meaning of 'logic'—mathematics is an extension of logic, some or all of mathematics is reducible to logic, or some or all of mathematics may be modelled in logic. Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead championed this programme, initiated by Gottlob Frege and subsequently developed by Richard Dedekind and Giuseppe Peano.
## Overview

Dedekind's path to logicism had a turning point when he was able to construct a model satisfying the axioms characterizing the real numbers using certain sets of rational numbers. This and related ideas convinced him that arithmetic, algebra and analysis were reducible to the natural numbers plus a "logic" of classes. Furthermore, by 1872 he had concluded that the naturals themselves were reducible to sets and mappings. It is likely that other logicists, most importantly Frege, were also guided by the new theories of the real numbers published in the year 1872 in Dedekind's Continuity and Irrational Numbers.

The philosophical impetus behind Frege's logicist programme from Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik (1884) onward was in part his dissatisfaction with the epistemological and ontological commitments of then-extant accounts of the natural numbers, and his conviction that Kant's use of truths about the natural numbers as examples of synthetic a priori truth was incorrect.

This started a period of expansion for logicism, with Dedekind and Frege as its main exponents. However, this initial phase of the logicist programme was brought into crisis with the discovery of the classical paradoxes of set theory (Cantor's 1896, Zermelo and Russell's 1900–1901). Frege gave up on the project after Russell recognized and communicated his paradox identifying an inconsistency in Frege's system set out in Grundgesetze der Arithmetik. Note that naive set theory also suffers from this difficulty.

On the other hand, Russell wrote The Principles of Mathematics in 1903 using the paradox and developments of Giuseppe Peano's school of geometry. Since he treated the subject of primitive notions in geometry and set theory

as well as the calculus of relations, this text is a watershed in the development of logicism. Evidence of the assertion of logicism was collected by Russell and Whitehead in their Principia Mathematica.

Today, the bulk of extant mathematics is believed to be derivable logically from a small number of extralogical axioms, such as the axioms of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory (or its extension ZFC), from which no inconsistencies have as yet been derived. Thus, elements of the logicist programmes have proved viable, but in the process theories of classes, sets and mappings, and higher-order logics other than with Henkin semantics have come to be regarded as extralogical in nature, in part under the influence of Quine's later thought.

Kurt Gödel's incompleteness theorems show that no formal system from which the Peano axioms for the natural numbers may be derived—such as Russell's systems in PM—can decide all the well-formed sentences of that system. This result damaged David Hilbert's programme for foundations of mathematics whereby 'infinitary' theories—such as that of PM—were to be proved consistent from finitary theories, with the aim that those uneasy about 'infinitary methods' could be reassured that their use should provably not result in the derivation of a contradiction. Gödel's result suggests that in order to maintain a logicist position, while still retaining as much as possible of classical mathematics, one must accept some axiom of infinity as part of logic. On the face of it, this damages the logicist programme also, albeit only for those already doubtful concerning 'infinitary methods'. Nonetheless, positions deriving from both logicism and from Hilbertian finitism have continued to be propounded since the publication of Gödel's result.

One argument that programmes derived from logicism remain valid might be that the incompleteness theorems are 'proved with logic just like any other theorems'. However, that argument appears not to acknowledge the distinction between theorems of first-order logic and theorems of higher-order logic. The former can be proven using finistic methods, while the latter—in general—cannot. Tarski's undefinability theorem shows that Gödel numbering can be used to prove syntactical constructs, but not semantic assertions. Therefore, the claim that logicism remains a valid programme may commit one to holding that a system of proof based on the existence and properties of the natural numbers is less convincing than one based on some particular formal system.
Logicism—especially through the influence of Frege on Russell and Wittgenstein and later Dummett—was a significant contributor to the development of analytic philosophy during the twentieth century.
## Origin of the name 'logicism'

Ivor Grattan-Guinness states that the French word 'Logistique' was "introduced by Couturat and others at the 1904 International Congress of Philosophy, and was used by Russell and others from then on, in versions appropriate for various languages." (G-G 2000:501).

Apparently the first (and only) usage by Russell appeared in his 1919: "Russell referred several time [sic] to Frege, introducing him as one 'who first succeeded in "logicising" mathematics' (p. 7). Apart from the misrepresentation (which Russell partly rectified by explaining his own view of the role of arithmetic in mathematics), the passage is notable for the word which he put in quotation marks, but their presence suggests nervousness, and he never used the word again, so that 'logicism' did not emerge until the later 1920s" (G-G 2002:434).

About the same time as Rudolf Carnap (1929), but apparently independently, Fraenkel (1928) used the word: "Without comment he used the name 'logicism' to characterise the Whitehead/Russell position (in the title of the section on p. 244, explanation on p. 263)" (G-G 2002:269). Carnap used a slightly different word 'Logistik'; Behmann complained about its use in Carnap's manuscript so Carnap proposed the word 'Logizismus', but he finally stuck to his word-choice 'Logistik' (G-G 2002:501). Ultimately "the spread was mainly due to Carnap, from 1930 onwards." (G-G 2000:502).
## Intent, or goal, of logicism

The overt intent of logicism is to derive all of mathematics from symbolic logic (Frege, Dedekind, Peano, Russell). As contrasted with algebraic logic (Boolean logic) that employs arithmetic concepts, symbolic logic begins with a very reduced set of marks (non-arithmetic symbols), a few "logical" axioms that embody the "laws of thought", and rules of inference that dictate how the marks are to be assembled and manipulated—for instance substitution and modus ponens (that is from A materially implies B and A, one may derive B). Logicism also adopts from Frege's groundwork the reduction of natural language statements from "subject|predicate" into either propositional "atoms" or the "argument|function" of "generalization"—the notions "all", "some", "class" (collection, aggregate) and "relation".

In a logicist derivation of the natural numbers and their properties, no "intuition" of number should "sneak in" either as an axiom or by accident. The goal is to derive all of mathematics, starting with the counting numbers and then the real numbers, from some chosen "laws of thought" alone, without any tacit assumptions of "before" and "after" or "less" and "more" or to the point: "successor" and "predecessor". Gödel 1944 summarized Russell's logicistic "constructions", when compared to "constructions" in the foundational systems of Intuitionism and Formalism ("the Hilbert School") as follows: "Both of these schools base their constructions on a mathematical intuition whose avoidance is exactly one of the principal aims of Russell's constructivism" (Gödel 1944 in Collected Works 1990:119).
## History

Gödel 1944 summarized the historical background from Leibniz's in Characteristica universalis, through Frege and Peano to Russell: "Frege was chiefly interested in the analysis of thought and used his calculus in the first place for deriving arithmetic from pure logic", whereas Peano "was more interested in its applications within mathematics". But "It was only [Russell's] Principia Mathematica that full use was made of the new method for actually deriving large parts of mathematics from a very few logical concepts and axioms. In addition, the young science was enriched by a new instrument, the abstract theory of relations" (pp. 120–121).

Kleene 1952 states it this way: "Leibniz (1666) first conceived of logic as a science containing the ideas and principles underlying all other sciences. Dedekind (1888) and Frege (1884, 1893, 1903) were engaged in defining mathematical notions in terms of logical ones, and Peano (1889, 1894–1908) in expressing mathematical theorems in a logical symbolism" (p. 43); in the previous paragraph he includes Russell and Whitehead as exemplars of the "logicistic school", the other two "foundational" schools being the intuitionistic and the "formalistic or axiomatic school" (p. 43).
Frege 1879 describes his intent in the Preface to his 1879 Begriffsschrift: He started with a consideration of arithmetic: did it derive from "logic" or from "facts of experience"?

I first had to ascertain how far one could proceed in arithmetic by means of inferences alone, with the sole support of those laws of thought that transcend all particulars. My initial step was to attempt to reduce the concept of ordering in a sequence to that of logical consequence, so as to proceed from there to the concept of number. To prevent anything intuitive from penetrating here unnoticed I had to bend every effort to keep the chain of inferences free of gaps... I found the inadequacy of language to be an obstacle; no matter how unwieldy the expressions I was ready to accept, I was less and less able, as the relations became more and more complex, to attain the precision that my purpose required. This deficiency led me to the idea of the present ideography. Its first purpose, therefore, is to provide us with the most reliable test of the validity of a chain of inferences and to point out every presupposition that tries to sneak in unnoticed.

Dedekind 1887 describes his intent in the 1887 Preface to the First Edition of his The Nature and Meaning of Numbers. He believed that in the "foundations of the simplest science; viz., that part of logic which deals with the theory of numbers" had not been properly argued—"nothing capable of proof ought to be accepted without proof":

In speaking of arithmetic (algebra, analysis) as a part of logic I mean to imply that I consider the number-concept entirely independent of the notions of intuitions of space and time, that I consider it an immediate result from the laws of thought... numbers are free creations of the human mind... [and] only through the purely logical process of building up the science of numbers... are we prepared accurately to investigate our notions of space and time by bringing them into relation with this number-domain created in our mind.
— Dedekind 1887 (Dover republication 1963:31)
Peano 1889 states his intent in his Preface to his 1889 Principles of Arithmetic:

Questions that pertain to the foundations of mathematics, although treated by many in recent times, still lack a satisfactory solution. The difficulty has its main source in the ambiguity of language.
That is why it is of the utmost importance to examine attentively the very words we use. My goal has been to undertake this examination.
Russell 1903 describes his intent in the Preface to his 1903 Principles of Mathematics:

The present work has two main objects. One of these, the proof that all pure mathematics deals exclusively with concepts definable in terms of a very small number of fundamental logical concepts, and that all its propositions are deducible from a very small number of fundamental logical principles.

A few words as to the origin of the present work may serve to show the importance of the questions discussed. About six years ago, I began an investigation into the philosophy of Dynamics.... [From two questions—acceleration and absolute motion in a "relational theory of space"] I was led to a re-examination of the principles of Geometry, thence to the philosophy of continuity and infinity, and then, with a view to discovering the meaning of the word any, to Symbolic Logic.
— Preface 1903:vi-vii

The * indicates a footnote where he states that:
Kronecker not long ago (Crelle's Journal, Vol. 99, pp. 334–336) has endeavored to impose certain limitations upon the free formation of concepts in mathematics which I do not believe to be justified.
Indeed he awaits Kronecker's "publishing his reasons for the necessity or merely the expediency of these limitations" (p. 45).

Kronecker, famous for his assertion that "God made the integers, all else is the work of man" had his foes, among them Hilbert. Hilbert called Kronecker a "dogmatist, to the extent that he accepts the integer with its essential properties as a dogma and does not look back" and equated his extreme constructivist stance with that of Brouwer's intuitionism, accusing both of "subjectivism": "It is part of the task of science to liberate us from arbitrariness, sentiment and habit and to protect us from the subjectivism that already made itself felt in Kronecker's views and, it seems to me, finds its culmination in intuitionism". Hilbert then states that "mathematics is a presuppositionless science. To found it I do not need God, as does Kronecker" (p. 479).

Russell's realism served him as an antidote to British idealism, with portions borrowed from European rationalism and British empiricism. To begin with, "Russell was a realist about two key issues: universals and material objects" (Russell 1912:xi). For Russell, tables are real things that exist independent of Russell the observer. Rationalism would contribute the notion of a priori knowledge, while empiricism would contribute the role of experiential knowledge (induction from experience). Russell would credit Kant with the idea of "a priori" knowledge, but he offers an objection to Kant he deems "fatal": "The facts [of the world] must always conform to logic and arithmetic. To say that logic and arithmetic are contributed by us does not account for this" (1912:87); Russell concludes that the a priori knowledge that we possess is "about things, and not merely about thoughts" (1912:89). And in this Russell's epistemology seems different from that of Dedekind's belief that "numbers are free creations of the human mind" (Dedekind 1887:31).

But his epistemology about the innate (he prefers the word a priori when applied to logical principles, cf. 1912:74) is intricate. He would strongly, unambiguously express support for the Platonic "universals" (cf. 1912:91–118) and he would conclude that truth and falsity are "out there"; minds create beliefs and what makes a belief true is a fact, "and this fact does not (except in exceptional cases) involve the mind of the person who has the belief" (1912:130).

Where did Russell derive these epistemic notions? He tells us in the Preface to his 1903 Principles of Mathematics. Note that he asserts that the belief "Emily is a rabbit" is non-existent, and yet the truth of this non-existent proposition is independent of any knowing mind; if Emily really is a rabbit, the fact of this truth exists whether or not Russell or any other mind is alive or dead, and the relation of Emily to rabbit-hood is "ultimate":

On fundamental questions of philosophy, my position, in all its chief features, is derived from Mr G. E. Moore. I have accepted from him the non-existential nature of propositions (except such as happen to assert existence) and their independence of any knowing mind; also the pluralism which regards the world, both that of existents and that of entities, as composed of an infinite number of mutually independent entities, with relations which are ultimate, and not reducible to adjectives of their terms or of the whole which these compose.... The doctrines just mentioned are, in my opinion, quite indispensable to any even tolerably satisfactory philosophy of mathematics, as I hope the following pages will show.... Formally, my premisses are simply assumed; but the fact that they allow mathematics to be true, which most current philosophies do not, is surely a powerful argument in their favour.
— Preface 1903:viii

In 1902 Russell discovered a "vicious circle" (Russell's paradox) in Frege's Grundgesetze der Arithmetik, derived from Frege's Basic Law V, and he was determined not to repeat it in his 1903 Principles of Mathematics. In two Appendices added at the last minute he devoted 28 pages to both a detailed analysis of Frege's theory contrasted against his own, and a fix for the paradox. But he was not optimistic about the outcome:

In the case of classes, I must confess, I have failed to perceive any concept fulfilling the conditions requisite for the notion of class. And the contradiction discussed in Chapter x. proves that something is amiss, but what this is I have hitherto failed to discover.
— Preface to Russell 1903:vi

Gödel in his 1944 would disagree with the young Russell of 1903 ("[my premisses] allow mathematics to be true") but would probably agree with Russell's statement quoted above ("something is amiss"); Russell's theory had failed to arrive at a satisfactory foundation of mathematics: the result was "essentially negative; that is the classes and concepts introduced this way do not have all the properties required for the use of mathematics" (Gödel 1944:132).

How did Russell arrive in this situation? Gödel observes that Russell is a surprising "realist" with a twist: he cites Russell's 1919:169 "Logic is concerned with the real world just as truly as zoology" (Gödel 1944:120). But he observes that "when he started on a concrete problem, the objects to be analyzed (for example the classes or propositions) soon for the most part turned into "logical fictions... [meaning] only that we have no direct perception of them" (Gödel 1944:120).

In an observation pertinent to Russell's brand of logicism, Perry remarks that Russell went through three phases of realism: extreme, moderate and constructive (Perry 1997:xxv). In 1903 he was in his extreme phase; by 1905 he would be in his moderate phase. In a few years he would "dispense with physical or material objects as basic bits of the furniture of the world. He would attempt to construct them out of sense-data" in his next book Our knowledge of the External World " (Perry 1997:xxvi).
These constructions in what Gödel 1944 would call "nominalistic constructivism... which might better be called fictionalism" derived from Russell's "more radical idea, the no-class theory" (p. 125):

"according to which classes or concepts never exist as real objects, and sentences containing these terms are meaningful only as they can be interpreted as... a manner of speaking about other things" (p. 125).

## An example of a logicist construction of the natural numbers: Russell's construction in the Principia

The logicism of Frege and Dedekind is similar to that of Russell, but with differences in the particulars (see Criticisms, below). Overall, the logicist derivations of the natural numbers are different from derivations from, for example, Zermelo's axioms for set theory ('Z'). Whereas, in derivations from Z, one definition of "number" uses an axiom of that system—the axiom of pairing—that leads to the definition of "ordered pair"—no overt number axiom exists in the various logicist axiom systems allowing the derivation of the natural numbers. Note that the axioms needed to derive the definition of a number may differ between axiom systems for set theory in any case. For instance, in ZF and ZFC, the axiom of pairing, and hence ultimately the notion of an ordered pair is derivable from the axiom of infinity and the axiom schema of replacement and is required in the definition of the von Neumann numerals (but not the Zermelo numerals), whereas in NFU the Frege numerals may be derived in an analogous way to their derivation in the Grundgesetze.

The Principia, like its forerunner the Grundgesetze, begins its construction of the numbers from primitive propositions such as "class", "propositional function", and in particular, relations of "similarity" ("equinumerosity": placing the elements of collections in one-to-one correspondence) and "ordering" (using "the successor of" relation to order the collections of the equinumerous classes)". The logicistic derivation equates the cardinal numbers constructed this way to the natural numbers, and these numbers end up all of the same "type"—as classes of classes—whereas in some set theoretical constructions—for instance the von Neumann and the Zermelo numerals—each number has its predecessor as a subset. Kleene observes the following.

The viewpoint here is very different from that of [Kronecker]'s maxim that 'God made the integers' plus Peano's axioms of number and mathematical induction], where we presupposed an intuitive conception of the natural number sequence, and elicited from it the principle that, whenever a particular property P of natural numbers is given such that (1) and (2), then any given natural number must have the property P.

The importance to the logicist programme of the construction of the natural numbers derives from Russell's contention "That all traditional pure mathematics can be derived from the natural numbers is a fairly recent discovery, though it had long been suspected" (1919:4). One derivation of the real numbers derives from the theory of Dedekind cuts on the rational numbers, rational numbers in turn being derived from the naturals. While an example of how this is done is useful, it relies first on the derivation of the natural numbers. So, if philosophical difficulties appear in a logicist derivation of the natural numbers, these problems should be sufficient to stop the program until these are resolved (see Criticisms, below).

For Russell, collections (classes) are aggregates of "things" specified by proper names, that come about as the result of propositions (assertions of fact about a thing or things). Russell analysed this general notion. He begins with "terms" in sentences, which he analysed as follows:
For Russell, "terms" are either "things" or "concepts":

Whatever may be an object of thought, or may occur in any true or false proposition, or can be counted as one, I call a term. This, then, is the widest word in the philosophical vocabulary. I shall use as synonymous with it the words, unit, individual, and entity. The first two emphasize the fact that every term is one, while the third is derived from the fact that every term has being, that is is in some sense. A man, a moment, a number, a class, a relation, a chimaera, or anything else that can be mentioned, is sure to be a term; and to deny that such and such a thing is a term must always be false.

Among terms, it is possible to distinguish two kinds, which I shall call respectively things and concepts; the former are the terms indicated by proper names, the latter those indicated by all other words... Among concepts, again, two kinds at least must be distinguished, namely those indicated by adjectives and those indicated by verbs.
The former kind will often be called predicates or class-concepts; the latter are always or almost always relations.

I shall speak of the terms of a proposition as those terms, however numerous, which occur in a proposition and may be regarded as subjects about which the proposition is. It is a characteristic of the terms of a proposition that anyone of them may be replaced by any other entity without our ceasing to have a proposition. Thus we shall say that "Socrates is human" is a proposition having only one term; of the remaining component of the proposition, one is the verb, the other is a predicate.... Predicates, then, are concepts, other than verbs, which occur in propositions having only one term or subject.

Suppose one were to point to an object and say: "This object in front of me named 'Emily' is a woman." This is a proposition, an assertion of the speaker's belief, which is to be tested against the "facts" of the outer world: "Minds do not create truth or falsehood. ## The definition of the natural numbers
In the Prinicipia, the natural numbers derive from all propositions that can be asserted about any collection of entities. Russell makes this clear in the second (italicized) sentence below.

In the first place, numbers themselves form an infinite collection, and cannot therefore be defined by enumeration. In the second place, the collections having a given number of terms themselves presumably form an infinite collection: it is to be presumed, for example, that there are an infinite collection of trios in the world, for if this were not the case the total number of things in the world would be finite, which, though possible, seems unlikely. In the third place, we wish to define "number" in such a way that infinite numbers may be possible; thus we must be able to speak of the number of terms in an infinite collection, and such a collection must be defined by intension, that is by a property common to all its members and peculiar to them.

To illustrate, consider the following finite example: Suppose there are 12 families on a street. Some have children, some do not. To discuss the names of the children in these households requires 12 propositions asserting "childname is the name of a child in family Fn" applied to this collection of households on the particular street of families with names F1, F2,.. F12. Each of the 12 propositions regards whether or not the "argument" childname applies to a child in a particular household. The children's names (childname) can be thought of as the x in a propositional function f(x), where the function is "name of a child in the family with name Fn".

Whereas the preceding example is finite over the finite propositional function "childnames of the children in family Fn'" on the finite street of a finite number of families, Russell apparently intended the following to extend to all propositional functions extending over an infinite domain so as to allow the creation of all the numbers.

Kleene considers that Russell has set out an impredicative definition that he will have to resolve, or risk deriving something like the Russell paradox. "Here instead we presuppose the totality of all properties of cardinal numbers, as existing in logic, prior to the definition of the natural number sequence" (Kleene 1952:44). The problem will appear, even in the finite example presented here, when Russell deals with the unit class (cf. Russell 1903:517).

The question arises what precisely a "class" is or should be. For Dedekind and Frege, a class is a distinct entity in its own right, a 'unity' that can be identified with all those entities x that satisfy some propositional function F. (This symbolism appears in Russell, attributed there to Frege: "The essence of a function is what is left when the x is taken away, i. e in the above instance, 2 +. The argument x does not belong to the function, but the two together make a whole (ib. p. 6 [that is Frege's 1891 Function und Begriff]" (Russell 1903:505).) For example, a particular "unity" could be given a name; suppose a family has the children with the names Annie, Barbie and Charles:

This notion of collection or class as object, when used without restriction, results in Russell's paradox; see more below about impredicative definitions. Russell's solution was to define the notion of a class to be only those elements that satisfy the proposition, his argument being that, indeed, the arguments x do not belong to the propositional function aka "class" created by the function. The class itself is not to be regarded as a unitary object in its own right, it exists only as a kind of useful fiction: "We have avoided the decision as to whether a class of things has in any sense an existence as one object. A decision of this question in either way is indifferent to our logic" (Principia Mathematica 1st ed. 1927:24).
Russell continues to hold this opinion in his 1919; observe the words "symbolic fictions":

When we have decided that classes cannot be things of the same sort as their members, that they cannot be just heaps or aggregates, and also that they cannot be identified with propositional functions, it becomes very difficult to see what they can be, if they are to be more than symbolic fictions. And if we can find any way of dealing with them as symbolic fictions, we increase the logical security of our position, since we avoid the need of assuming that there are classes without being compelled to make the opposite assumption that there are no classes. We merely abstain from both assumptions.... But when we refuse to assert that there are classes, we must not be supposed to be asserting dogmatically that there are none. We are merely agnostic as regards them...
